rv.q: There are also, it has to be said, some really clumsy moments in a debut that’s too long, at two hours plus interval, for its experimental form.
While Baghdaddy’s complicated parts do not quite come together, its boldness is extraordinary and certainly showcases the playwright’s fearless talent.
‘Baghdaddy’ is a genuinely promising debut that very much feels like the work of an early years playwright and might have been better served by the Court’s smaller Upstairs theatre.
Too much biographical and political detail goes missing in action.
Baghdaddy doesn’t become diatribe but it does pack a punch that may leave you reeling.
It is a shame that the force and vivacity of the writing is stifled by direction that is too eager to please.
In places, it fudges essential dramatic choices; leading to an uneven, but nonetheless interesting, production.

Steeped in a roiling mixture of grievance and affection, the play comes movingly to a close on a straightforwardly expressed “thanks Dad” - proof positive that for all life’s lacerations, what will survive of us with any luck is love.
At best Baghdaddy is a surreal trip into traumatic memory, at its worst it’s a self-indulgent mess.
This is a powerful exploration of inter-generational trauma, boldly staged by Milli Bhatia.
The comedy distracts, rather than accentuates.
It is, quite simply, a necessary story, beautifully told – something the Royal Court has excelled at of late.

cn.t: Jones' semi-autobiographical debut about intergenerational trauma earns praise for its emotional power and originality, but critics remain divided on its absurdist staging and uneven execution.
